title: ETS 06 — Service Anomaly Investigation
description: Incident commander full investigation view — combines metrics, traces, logs, and profiles in one place. Follow the five steps in order: STEP 1 DETECT: Which route and replica is generating 500s? The 5xx table shows route×replica×status with exact counts. STEP 2 BOOKING DEPS: Is the failure in Redis gate, DB lock, or a specific booking stage? STEP 3 TRACE: Use the Traces panel to find a failing trace. Click the trace to open the waterfall view. In the trace detail, click 'Node Graph' to see the ingress→booking→postgres call chain as a visual dependency graph. Each node shows service.name and service.instance.id — this tells you exactly which of the 3 backend replicas handled the failing request. From the trace, click 'Logs for this trace' to jump to Loki logs correlated by otel_trace_id. STEP 4 LOGS: Recent error logs from all backend replicas filtered to level=error. The otel_trace_id field is a clickable link back to Tempo. STEP 5 PROFILE: CPU profile activity by service. From a trace, click 'Profiles for this span' to open the Pyroscope CPU flamegraph scoped to the exact time window of the failing request.

panels.title: ▶ STEP 0 — TOPOLOGY: Full nginx → backend call chain (e2e trace map)
E2E Traces — click any trace → open Node Graph for full nginx → frontend → backend → postgres chain
panels.description: Recent traces rooted at cets-edge-lb showing the full ingress path. Click any trace row to open the span waterfall in Tempo. In the trace detail view, click 'Node Graph' to see the visual dependency graph: cets-edge-lb → cets-gateway-{1,2,3} → cets-frontend-lb → cets-frontend-{1,2,3} → cets-backend-lb → cets-backend → postgres. Each node shows the service name — the gateway and frontend nodes include the replica number so you can identify exactly which instance handled the request. The Node Graph uses parent-child span relationships (not the aggregated service graph metrics) and shows the complete chain even for nginx SERVER-only spans.

panels.title: Backend → Postgres Service Graph (CLIENT span edges)
panels.description: Aggregated service dependency graph from Tempo's metrics generator. Shows edges where the Go backend makes CLIENT-kind calls to PostgreSQL. The nginx proxy tiers are not shown here because nginx only produces SERVER spans — use the per-trace Node Graph (click a trace in the left panel) for the full nginx → frontend → backend chain.

panels.title: ▶ STEP 1 — DETECT: Which route and replica is generating 500s?
5xx Error Rate by Route × Replica
panels.description: 5xx request rate broken down by route and replica. Each series is labelled 'route replica' so you can immediately see which backend instance (backend-1, backend-2, backend-3) is the error source. A single replica producing all errors while others are healthy = instance-specific fault. Set $replica to that value to narrow all other panels.

panels.title: 5xx Total Last 5 min
panels.description: Total 5xx count in the current window. Non-zero means something is actively broken.

panels.title: P99 Latency Last 5 min
panels.description: Current P99 latency. High latency with low error rate = slow path (DB contention, Redis slow). High latency with high error rate = fast failure storm.

panels.title: 5xx Count — Route × Replica × Status (last 5 min)
panels.description: Exact 5xx counts in the current window sorted by count descending. The 'replica' column is the key — it tells you which backend-1/backend-2/backend-3 is responsible. Use this to set $replica to the affected instance before proceeding to STEP 3 traces.

panels.title: ▶ STEP 2 — BOOKING DEPS: Is Redis, DB lock, or a specific booking stage the cause?
Booking Stage Error Rate by Stage
panels.description: Rate of booking stage observations where outcome=error, per stage. A spike on 'preadmission' = Redis gate failure. A spike on 'capacity' = capacity check error (not just exhausted). A spike on 'commit' = PostgreSQL transaction failure. This narrows the STEP 3 trace search to the correct span type.

panels.title: Redis Gate Errors by Operation × Outage Mode
panels.description: Rate of Redis gate errors, broken down by operation (reserve/release/commit) and outage mode. outage_mode=fail means bookings are being rejected because of Redis. outage_mode=degrade means Redis is slow but bookings continue. No data here = Redis is not the problem.

panels.title: DB Lock Waiting Sessions
panels.description: PostgreSQL sessions blocked on a lock. Any value > 0 means booking transactions are blocking each other. Lock contention causes acquire_wait to rise which causes pool saturation which causes 500s. This is a common root cause for backend-specific error spikes.

panels.title: DB Pool Acquire Wait by Backend Instance
panels.description: Average time spent waiting for a DB connection from the pool, per backend replica. A single replica with high acquire wait = that replica's pool is saturated. Combine with the 5xx table above: if backend-2 has both errors and high acquire wait, the pool is the bottleneck.

panels.title: Booking Stage P95 (all stages)
panels.description: P95 latency for every booking stage. Combine with the error rate panel: if 'commit' is both slow AND erroring, it is the failing transaction. If only 'preadmission' is slow, Redis is degraded but not erroring.

panels.title: ▶ STEP 3 — TRACE: Find the failing request. Use Node Graph to identify the replica.
Service Dependency Graph
panels.description: Visual topology of service calls generated from Tempo span metrics. Edges show client→server call direction with request rate and error rate. A red edge = errors on that call path. Click a node to see its metrics. This is the service-level view — for per-request per-replica detail, click a trace in the Traces panel and then click 'Node Graph' inside the trace view.

panels.title: Recent Error Traces (click to open waterfall + Node Graph)
panels.description: Traces from cets-* services where status=error, from the selected time window. Click any trace row to open the full span waterfall in Tempo. In the trace detail, click 'Node Graph' to see the ingress→backend→postgres dependency graph for that specific request. The resource.service.instance.id attribute on each span shows exactly which replica (backend-1, backend-2, backend-3) handled the request. Use 'Logs for this trace' to jump to Loki. Use 'Profiles for this span' to open Pyroscope.

panels.title: ▶ STEP 4 — LOGS: Correlate structured error logs with otel_trace_id
Backend Error Logs (level=error, all replicas)
panels.description: Structured JSON logs from backend-1/2/3 and worker processes filtered to level=error. Each log line includes otel_trace_id — click the underlined trace ID link to jump directly to that trace in Tempo. The 'replica' field shows which backend instance logged the error. The 'route', 'stage', and 'outcome' fields help correlate with the metrics panels above without needing a trace.

panels.title: Trace-Correlated Logs (requests with otel_trace_id)
panels.description: All backend log lines that include an otel_trace_id field — these are requests that were actively traced. Use this when looking for logs for a specific trace that you found in Tempo but haven't found in the error logs panel (the request may have succeeded but been slow).

panels.title: ▶ STEP 5 — PROFILE: CPU & memory hotspots per service
CPU Profile Timeline (Pyroscope)
panels.description: CPU nanoseconds consumed over time per cets-* service. Non-zero confirms the profiler is running. Use this timeline to identify WHEN a CPU spike occurred, then scroll down to the flamegraphs to see WHAT code was hot during that window.

panels.title: CPU Flamegraph
panels.description: Interactive CPU flamegraph aggregated across all cets-* services. Each bar represents a function — wider bars consume more CPU. Click a bar to zoom into that call subtree. Use the search box to filter (e.g. 'pgx' for database, 'redis' for cache). Select a narrower time range to scope the flamegraph to a specific incident window.

panels.title: Memory Allocation Flamegraph
panels.description: Interactive memory allocation flamegraph showing which functions allocate the most heap memory. Useful for diagnosing memory pressure, GC overhead, or OOM-killed containers. Wide bars = high allocation rate. Filter with 'json' for serialization hotspots or 'pgx' for database result scanning.
